newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower before 10-yr T-note sale.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower before 10-yr T-note sale.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities opened lower on Wednesday ahead of the Treasury's afternoon auction of $12 billion of 10-year securities.
The 10-year note auction, the second and last part of the Treasury's quarterly refunding effort, comes on the heels of Tuesday's disappointing $17.0 billion three-year note sale.

Analysts said the market was under pressure from new supply, from the need to reduce prices to attract bidders to Wednesday's 10-year Treasury note auction, and from the unwinding of some curve-flattening trades.

While the 10-year Treasury note auction is apt to be the main event of the trading session, the market will also get several economic reports, including the Federal Reserve's Beige Book anecdotal description of business conditions around the country.

"The Beige Book could say something damaging (to the market) in terms of strong demand but it won't find anything wrong with wages or prices because there's no inflation," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

While the Beige Book will not be available until an hour after the 1300 EDT/1700 GMT bidding deadline for the 10-year auction, the market will get data on March wholesale inventories and first-quarter productivity and unit labor costs at mid-morning.

First-quarter productivity, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, is expected to be up 2.4 percent with a 1.0 percent increase in unit labor costs, according to economists polled by Reuters. Those would be friendly figures for the bonds but Rupkey said any market reaction to them was likely to be slight.
March wholesale inventories, also due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT and expected to be up 0.4 percent, will also be a minor event, analysts said.
"The market looks at wholesale inventories a little bit," said Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "It's only one piece of the inventory puzzle."

"We're a little interested in wholesale inventories because inventories added a lot to GDP (Gross Domestic Product) in the first quarter," said Rupkey. "In the second quarter, they should subtract from GDP. This report will just help to clarify what happened in the first quarter."

The market is not expected to react to the Fed's consumer installment credit data, due at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters estimate that consumer installment credit totaled $6.7 billion in March, unchanged from February.
Analysts said a weaker dollar could also weigh on Treasury prices. The dollar opened lower on Wednesday with support said to be located at 124.50 yen and 1.7050 marks.
In early trade, the benchmark 30-year bond was down 8/32 to 96-13/32, yielding 6.91 percent. Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-4/32, yielding 6.31 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum, three-month bills were up two basis points to 5.07 percent. Six-month bills were up one basis point to 5.36 percent and year bills were up two basis points to 5.58 percent.
Five-year notes were off 3/32 to 100-06/32 to yield 6.58 percent and 10-years were down 5/32 at 96-28/32 to yield 6.69 percent.
The 10-year notes to be sold at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT were yielding 6.695 percent on a when-issued basis.
